items.title: Elon Musk confirms talks to merge Tesla and SpaceX
items.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.
items.content:
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.

"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.

While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."

With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.

The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.

That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.

SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.

Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X , the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.

Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.

Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.

He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.

Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".

He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".

Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.

While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.

SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

SpaceX shares sink after first earnings report reveals huge AI spending plans

items.title: Pakistan arrests man hunted by US over $126m postage fraud case
items.summary: Faheem Akram allegedly sold more than 5 million fake postage labels for a fixed price of $2 a piece.
items.content:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

items.title: ChatGPT nasconde le conversazioni private: arriva il blocco con PIN
items.summary: ChatGPT permette di nascondere le conversazioni con PIN o biometria, ma attenzione ai limiti.
items.content:
Il nostro rapporto con l'AI sta diventando sempre più intimo, a tal punto che non tutte le chat possono essere viste da chiunque. Ormai con l'AI si parla di tutto e nelle chat si scrive ogni cosa, ma questo nuovo modo di interagire se da un lato interessante, dall'altro fonte è di problemi, ad esempio di privacy. Ci sono sempre più informazioni personali nelle conversazioni con gli assistenti AI, che spaziano dalle questioni di salute ai problemi lavorativi, passando per documenti riservati e confidenze private, la cronologia di ChatGPT può raccontare parecchio di noi.

Pensateci, basta lasciare il computer sbloccato o prestare lo smartphone a qualcuno perché queste informazioni diventino facilmente accessibili. Ecco che per risolvere il problema OpenAI ha introdotto Locked Chats, una nuova funzione che permette di proteggere singole conversazioni attraverso un PIN di quattro cifre. Sugli smartphone compatibili è possibile utilizzare anche il riconoscimento biometrico, come Face ID o Touch ID, e tutto funziona in modo semplice. Dal menu di una conversazione basta selezionare l'opzione per bloccarla.

A quel punto, la chat scompare dalla normale cronologia, dalle conversazioni fissate in alto e dai risultati di ricerca. Rimane comunque accessibile attraverso una sezione dedicata, chiamata Locked chats, all'interno dei Progetti. La novità permette quindi di conservare le conversazioni più delicate senza doverle eliminare, mantenendole separate dalle altre.

items.title: La Finanza scopre la 'banca occulta' della criminalità organizzata, 30 arresti
items.summary: Coinvolti esponenti di 'ndrangheta, camorra e 'Quarta mafia'. Misura anche per l'autista dell'ufficio gip di Milano
items.content:
La Guardia di Finanza di Milano e Monza Brianza ha smantellato la "banca occulta" della criminalità organizzata in un'operazione che ha portato a 30 arresti e che vede coinvolti esponenti di 'ndrangheta, camorra e la cosiddetta "Quarta mafia" (la criminalità organizzata foggiana). Scoperti oltre 110 milioni di euro di fatture false e riciclaggio internazionale da 68 milioni di euro tramite criptovalute. Sono in corso, oltre ai 30 arresti, sequestri per 21 milioni di euro.

Tra gli arrestati nell'ambito dell'operazione vi è anche Domenico Bruno, un autista dell'ufficio gip di Milano che si occupava dei beni sotto sequestro e che è già coinvolto in un'altra indagine. In questa inchiesta Bruno, che è stato posto ai domiciliari, è accusato di accesso abusivo a sistema informatico. Nelle indagini è anche coinvolto un avvocato di Milano oltre a persone appartenenti alla criminalità organizzata.

I Finanzieri dei Comandi Provinciali di Milano e Monza Brianza, con il supporto del Servizio Centrale d'Investigazione sulla Criminalità Organizzata e del Nucleo Speciale Repressione Frodi Tecnologiche, su delega della DDA della Procura di Milano e in coordinamento con la Direzione Nazionale Antimafia e Antiterrorismo, stanno eseguendo un'ordinanza di misure cautelari nei confronti di 30 indagati, di cui 16 in carcere, 14 ai domiciliari, e un decreto di sequestro preventivo d'urgenza per oltre 21 milioni di euro.

L'operazione scaturisce da un'attività investigativa del Nucleo di Polizia Economico Finanziaria della Guardia di Finanza di Milano con il supporto del Gruppo di Monza, che ha di disarticolato un'associazione per delinquere aggravata dall'agevolazione e dal metodo mafioso, dedita al riciclaggio internazionale, alle frodi fiscali, ai reati fallimentari, al traffico di stupefacenti e a reati in materia di armi.

Arresti anche in Spagna e in Svizzera e perquisizioni in varie provincie italiane, con l'impiego di oltre 350 militari della Guardia di Finanza, oltre a unità specialistiche e della componente "AntiTerrorismo Pronto Impiego" del Corpo. Le operazioni in Spagna e Svizzera sono condotte con il supporto dell'Unità I-CAN (Interpol Cooperation Against 'Ndrangheta) del Servizio per la Cooperazione Internazionale di Polizia e in stretto contatto con gli Esperti per la Sicurezza della Direzione Centrale della Polizia Criminale di stanza a Madrid e Berna. Nel corso delle attività si sta procedendo al sequestro di denaro contante, conti correnti, criptovalute, autovetture, imbarcazioni, gioielli, orologi di lusso nonché macchinette conta soldi.

items.title: SpaceX vola con l'AI: ricavi in crescita del 161%

items.title: Battlezone Online: BZFlag in the Browser
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/timriker/bzo Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50176298 Points: 20 # Comments: 11
items.content:
A free 3D multiplayer tank game in the browser -- on a desktop, a phone or a VR headset -- that plays with BZFlag clients and servers. Nothing to install.

Play now: https://bz.rikers.org · Servers · Help: controls and flags · BZFlag Discord

https://bz.rikers.org/list lists the public bzo servers, and the BZFlag servers any of them proxies. Click a row to enter that game.

The server is Node.js; the client is Three.js, over WebSockets, WebTransport and WebRTC.

Every published image contains linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 variants. Release tags use stable vX.Y.Z SemVer only; prerelease and build-metadata tags are not published.

Docker images are built on Ubuntu 26.04 with Ubuntu's own nodejs package (Node.js 22), and CI runs on the same Node in an Ubuntu 26.04 container.

A Docker image from GitHub Container Registry, or a source tarball or git checkout. Docker is the better install and update path for most people.

docs/installation.md covers both, plus configuration, running behind a reverse proxy, listing your server, proxying BZFlag servers, and updating.

A site that polls servers -- stats, a server browser -- finds what it can ask in docs/api.md .

/list 's Launch links open a BZFlag server in an installed BZFlag client; docs/bzflag-links.md sets up bzflag:// on Linux, Windows and macOS.

bzo carries every flag BZFlag has. WA Wide Angle spawns, sticks and shakes off like any bad flag, but does nothing: it widens the field of view, and in VR the headset owns the projection.

docs/controls.md has every control: the keyboard and mouse, the on-screen touch controls, gamepads, and the XR controllers. In the game, / or ? shows the keyboard's.

The VR mode uses native WebXR and requires a browser and headset that support immersive-vr . For local validation, open the game at http://localhost:5154 . For remote access, serve the game over https:// -- with the server's own https certificate, or at a reverse proxy; the client automatically uses wss:// for its WebSocket connection when the page is served over HTTPS.

A headset browser launching the installed app tries to enter VR with no 2D landing page. xr-launch.js asks for the session before the rest of the client loads, and keeps asking on each signal that could carry the user activation an immersive session needs -- window load, focus, page show, visibility change, and the Launch Handler -- with the renderer picking up whichever session results. Where none of them lands, and everywhere else, VR Mode starts from the button.

A saved name joins immediately, and without one the XR menu opens on a Join screen carrying the same name, team, and tank choices as the 2D entry dialog, so nothing waits on a screen the player cannot see.

Typing in XR uses the headset's own system keyboard, raised when the Name or MOTD row takes focus. Quest Browser 26.1 and later provide one; a headset that does not marks those rows Desktop only, and the player can still join under the name the server assigns. Each time the keyboard opens it starts a fresh edit, so the first key replaces the whole field rather than appending to it.

The one-tap VR button beside the settings gear is shown only on a device with a headset, because Chrome on Android reports immersive-vr support on any phone through Cardboard; VR Mode stays in the Settings menu there.

If the deployment sets a restrictive Permissions-Policy header, allow xr-spatial-tracking=(self) . TLS is either the server's own ( https , see docs/installation.md ) or a reverse proxy's ( docs/installation.md ).

Use the WebXR validation checklist when checking a new browser, headset, or deployment. WebGPU rendering is outside the scope of this checklist.

This runs the syntax and lint checks, a server boot check, and the test suites.

Commit everything first, and leave nothing behind: a tag names a tree, so an edit still sitting in the working directory when the tag goes out is not in the release -- the version says one thing and the box says another, and nobody can reproduce it from the tag. That includes work somebody else left uncommitted: review it, say what it is, and commit it, rather than tagging around it. git status is clean before preparing a release and clean again once the tag is pushed; anything still pending at the end means the release went out without it.

Release tags are stable vX.Y.Z SemVer only -- prereleases and build metadata are not published.

All four go in the release commit. public/version.mjs is the one easy to leave behind, and a tag without it ships a client reporting the version before it.

Then edit the new changelog section so it contains the real user-visible changes.

The subject describes the release rather than labelling it: the version is already in the tag, package.json and CHANGELOG.md , and git log --oneline is the one view where the subject is all there is. Name the change in a few words and reference the issue with a real closing keyword where the release finishes it, since a bare (#NN) only links.

A release that fails its workflow is left alone. bzo is in development and not every tag produces artifacts. Fix the cause and move to the next version -- do not delete or move a published tag, and do not backfill a GitHub release for one that never built. CHANGELOG.md is the record either way, and it already carries the section for the version that failed.

public/version.mjs is written by scripts/prepare-release.mjs and verified against the tag by scripts/check-release.mjs . Do not edit it by hand, and do not reintroduce a hardcoded client version string elsewhere.

bzo ships models, textures, sounds and maps from several places: some are the BZFlag project's, used under its licence; some were made for bzo; some arrived with a contribution. A file does not inherit the repository's licence by sitting in it, and an asset whose origin nobody recorded is a question left for whoever asks next.

Not every asset already in the tree meets that bar. Some predate the expectation and some arrived with a contribution that was worth taking on its own merits, and the intent is to reach clear, recorded licensing for every one of them rather than to pretend it is already done. If you know the provenance of something here, or you are the author of it, please say so in an issue -- that is the cheapest way this gets finished.

Maps are the same question in a different shape: a map downloaded from a server, or saved out by a client, carries no grant with it. See docs/bzw.md for the map format itself.

items.title: Nexus-CLI – Pure Go Bridge to DeepSeek R1/V3 with Claude Code and Ollama Support
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/xamrayev/nexus-cli Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50176129 Points: 10 # Comments: 2
items.content:
A high-performance Golang CLI utility and local API proxy server that enables any application or coding agent to connect to DeepSeek V3 ( deepseek-chat ) and R1 ( deepseek-reasoner / Thinking) models via a free web account ( chat.deepseek.com ), without requiring an official paid DeepSeek API key.

Rewritten from scratch in pure Go (Golang) based on in-depth analysis of Node.js ( FreeDeepseekAPI-EN ) and Python ( deepseek_bridge ) projects, featuring zero runtime dependencies .

This automatically launches a Chrome window. Once you log in, Nexus securely captures and stores the session token.

You can now route any tool (Cursor, Open WebUI, Claude Code) to http://localhost:9655/v1 !

Nexus implements the Ollama API specification. Open WebUI, Dify, AnythingLLM, Cursor, LlamaIndex, and official Ollama libraries can connect directly to http://localhost:9655 :

Enforce strict JSON output or conform to a specified schema:

Launch coding tools and agents with a single command — Nexus automatically boots the proxy server in the background:

Avoid rate limits (HTTP 429) by cycling through multiple DeepSeek accounts using Round-Robin rotation:

items.title: Monte dei Paschi di Siena: the world’s oldest bank at the heart of Italy’s financial power struggle
items.summary: On 29 October, shareholders will decide the fate of the Tuscan bank, as Intesa Sanpaolo’s €35bn takeover bid derails Meloni’s nationalist ambitions for Italy’s banking sector
items.content:
She is a very, very old lady. But fate has decreed that, just as she passes the venerable age of 500, she should find herself caught up in enough adventures, misfortunes and dramatic twists to fill an entire lifetime.

Monte dei Paschi di Siena, the world's oldest bank, has gone from the brink of collapse to a state bailout in the space of just a few years, from prey to predator, only to find itself once again in the uncomfortable position of being hunted. Above all, it is now at the centre of the biggest battle for control of Italian finance.

The bank now appears destined to fall into the hands of Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank. The roughly €35bn offer launched in June by the group led by Carlo Messina looks increasingly difficult to resist. Meanwhile, an attempt by MPS chief executive Luigi Lovaglio to escape Intesa's embrace by acquiring two other banks has lost the backing of its main shareholders, including construction magnate and financier Francesco Gaetano Caltagirone and Delfin, the holding company of the turbulent Del Vecchio dynasty behind eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

One crucial hurdle remains: the shareholders' meeting on 29 October, which is expected to settle the matter once and for all. But the story already seems to be heading towards yet another reversal of fortune. The bank that took over Mediobanca barely a year ago now looks set to be taken over itself.

To understand how it came to this, we need to go back more than five centuries.

In 1472, the Republic of Siena established a Monte di Pietà, a charitable lending institution that provided small loans to the city's poorest residents.

Something of those origins has stayed with Monte dei Paschi ever since: an exceptionally close bond with Siena and its centers of power.

Siena, after all, is no ordinary place. Its 17 contrade, or historic districts, fight fiercely for victory in the Palio horse race, yet close ranks with remarkable determination whenever the city's interests need defending against outsiders.

For centuries, Monte dei Paschi was foremost among those interests. It funded universities and social programmes, provided jobs and distributed wealth. To the people of Siena, it was more than a bank: it was Babbo Monte, or "Papa Monte".

And as so often happens when banking interests become entangled with political calculations, things can go badly wrong.

That has been particularly true in recent decades. Siena has long been a stronghold of the left, first of the Communist and Socialist parties and later of the Democratic Party.

Through the Monte dei Paschi Foundation, which retained control of the bank even after its stock market flotation in 1999, local politicians continued to wield considerable influence over management decisions.

It was against this backdrop that the deal which changed everything took shape in 2007: the acquisition of Antonveneta.

Under chairman Giuseppe Mussari, a product of Siena's political establishment, Monte dei Paschi was determined to shed its provincial status and compete with the big players.

It paid Spain's Santander around €9bn for Banca Antonveneta, which the Spanish group had acquired only shortly before, during the break-up of the Dutch bank ABN Amro, for a much lower price.

It was November 2007, and the collapse of Lehman Brothers was approaching. Monte dei Paschi entered the global financial crisis with its finances already in a fragile state.

What followed was a succession of capital increases, non-performing loans, the sovereign debt crisis and a derivatives scandal involving Deutsche Bank and Nomura, which triggered years of investigations and court proceedings.

The foundation, which had borrowed heavily in an effort to retain control, lost almost all its assets.

The bank that had financed Siena for centuries was now in danger of going under.

The rescue came in 2017. The Italian state injected €8.2bn into the ailing bank, taking a stake of around 70%.

A prolonged restructuring followed, with thousands of job cuts and branches closures.

The recovery only began to take shape in 2022, with the arrival of Luigi Lovaglio as chief executive. No longer a young banker, Lovaglio nevertheless brought fresh drive to the institution.

A capital increase, cost-cutting, rising interest rates and the return of dividends helped turn the business around. In 2024, Monte dei Paschi posted almost €2bn in profits.

Giorgia Meloni's government, keen to return MPS to private ownership, began selling its shares — but not to just anyone.

In November 2024, the Treasury sold a 15% stake to a select group of investors: Banco BPM, Anima, Caltagirone and the holding company owned by the heirs of Leonardo Del Vecchio.

The identities of the buyers, however, tell much of the story.

Caltagirone and Delfin were already shareholders in Mediobanca and Generali, Italy's largest insurance group. For years, they had challenged the balance of power surrounding the two institutions, seeking to gain control of them.

Founded in 1946 by Enrico Cuccia, Mediobanca had exercised decisive influence over Italian capitalism for decades through a web of cross-shareholdings and relationships with the country's great industrial families.

Its crown jewel was its stake of around 13% in Generali, which, while not conferring formal control, effectively gave it control over the insurer.

And so Monte dei Paschi, rescued with taxpayers' money, became the instrument of a remarkable reversal in the balance of power.

In January 2025, Lovaglio, acting in full agreement with his new major shareholders — effectively handpicked by the Meloni government — dared to attempt the seemingly impossible: he launched a takeover bid for Mediobanca from Siena.

The Milan public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the government's sale of the MPS shares.

The bid was greeted with widespread scepticism. But eight months later, Lovaglio had won.

Monte dei Paschi now controlled the Milanese investment bank and, through Mediobanca, its stake in Generali. Caltagirone and Delfin, already direct shareholders in the insurer, emerged with even greater influence.

But that victory already contained the seeds of the next battle.

By acquiring Mediobanca, MPS gained the largest single shareholding in Generali, at 13.35%.

Generali operates in more than 50 countries, serves around 75 million customers and had €944bn in assets under management in mid-2026.

Acquiring Monte dei Paschi would not give Intesa control of Generali, whose shareholders also include Caltagirone, Delfin and UniCredit. But by combining Mediobanca's holding with the 3.13% it already owns, Intesa would become Generali's largest shareholder, with considerable influence over the insurer.

Lovaglio's counterstrategy was to expand MPS further, by acquiring Banco BPM and Banca Generali — a plan that would almost double the group's size.

But Crédit Agricole, Banco BPM's largest shareholder, opposed the move, while Caltagirone and Delfin distanced themselves from the plan.

Intesa then raised the stakes, making its offer conditional on Monte dei Paschi shareholders rejecting Lovaglio's proposal.

The shareholders will make their decision official on 29 October, but an Intesa victory is no longer in doubt.

After more than five centuries of history, Monte dei Paschi looks set to retain its name but lose its independence.

The Meloni government had hoped to use Caltagirone and Delfin to create a "third force" in Italian banking, giving financial substance to its nationalist ambitions.

Instead, it is effectively being forced to bow to the rules of the market — where, ultimately, those with the deepest pockets prevail.

For years, the Italian right held up Monte dei Paschi as a symbol of the damage caused by the cosy relationship between left-wing politics and banking.

Now, after a right-wing government helped bring major private investors back into the bank's ownership, Intesa's plan envisages transferring a large proportion of the bank's branches in Siena to Unipol and then to its subsidiary BPER.

And Unipol is controlled by the cooperative movement, heir to the so-called red cooperatives historically associated with the Italian left.

If this was supposed to be a triumph for the government's brand of financial nationalism, things have certainly not gone according to plan.

items.title: From washing glasses to gardening guru: meet Spicy Moustache, the Italian with 6.4 million followers
items.summary: Alessandro Vitale once dreamed of becoming a tattoo artist. Instead, he began turning London balconies and rooftops into gardens, building a new life around growing food, composting and reducing waste
items.content:
With his muscular build and tattoos covering much of his body, Alessandro Vitale, better known online as Spicy Moustache, looks as though he belongs on a rock stage or in a tattoo studio.

Instead, this young man from Verona, who has amassed 6.4 million followers on Instagram, has built his own kind of revolution around soil, compost and banana peels.

It all goes back to his roots. "My first real connection with nature came through my grandfather, who taught me about farming and respect for the land, and my grandmother, who passed on her love of wholesome cooking. Between them, there was an unspoken golden rule: nothing goes to waste. Everything goes back into the cycle."

After leaving Italy at 23, he worked his way up from washing glasses in London's pubs while dreaming of becoming a full-time tattoo artist. But above all, it was in the British capital that he rediscovered the deep-rooted need for green space he had always felt.

He began growing plants wherever he could: on balconies, rooftops and in the tiniest of courtyards. From there, he built an entirely new life.

His first videos, posted in late 2018, focused on growing hot peppers, hence his online name.

Today, he lives in Ibiza and has become a social media phenomenon, bringing sustainability and self-sufficient living to a mass audience.

Let's start at the beginning. Why did you leave Italy, and how did you end up in London?

"I was making handmade shoes near Verona. I wanted a change. I didn't want to feel obliged to take a permanent job just for the sake of security. So, at 23, I left for London. The impact of arriving in such a huge city was traumatic: the frantic pace, the language barrier, the stress.

I wanted to become a tattoo artist, but I ended up working in bars. Within eight months, thanks to London's meritocratic culture, I went from washing glasses to becoming a general manager.

Then, because of the cost of rent, I had to move house six times in five years. I turned every move into an opportunity, creating gardens on balconies, rooftops and in courtyards, learning from my mistakes along the way."

Where does your deep connection with the land and cooking come from?

"From my grandparents, who lived in San Bonifacio, near Verona. My grandfather used to take me fishing, mushroom picking and gathering wild asparagus. We made olive oil and wine together. My grandmother taught me to make the most of simple ingredients.

But above all, waste simply wasn't part of their vocabulary. Everything that came out of the vegetable garden went back into a closed cycle, between the kitchen and the compost heap.

When our content took off on social media in 2021, following a BBC documentary, I realised I wanted to carry those same values forward, but this time reach the whole world by communicating in English."

Your videos last just a few seconds, but they're meticulously produced. How much work goes into them?

"A 30- to 50-second video takes two to three days of work. I research the ingredient, look for food scraps that everyone has at home, such as banana peels or leftover rice, and work out how to transform them into something fun, simple and easy to recreate.

The idea is to ‘market sustainability’: to take a serious, meaningful concept and turn it into something engaging."

Beyond cooking and gardening, what other areas are you exploring?

"We've expanded from permaculture and low-waste cooking into natural personal care products. Plants are the foundation of medicine. We're launching a skin balm made from flowers harvested in our garden and left to macerate for 30 days.

What's more, for every pack sold, we'll fund tree planting. The packaging is made from paper embedded with seeds that can be planted to support bees."

After London, you're now working from Ibiza. How has the move changed the way you work?

"In London, I was always rushing around. Here, I focus on my mental and physical wellbeing. I don't touch my smartphone for the first two hours of the morning.

I go out into the garden, soak up some sun, look after the chickens and check on the seeds. That immediate connection with nature sets the rhythm of my day before my phone notifications do."

"Having a real impact on people's lives. I'm not interested in becoming a billionaire. What keeps me going is when people write to me saying things like, 'Thanks to you, I've stopped throwing away coffee grounds,' or 'I've planted basil on my balcony.'

When I lived in London, I used to invite a four-year-old boy into my garden and give him strawberries and seedlings. Passing this passion on to younger generations is an indescribable feeling."

And you've shared this success with your partner throughout...

"We've been together for 11 years, and I wouldn't be where I am today without her. She believed in me more than I did. She's now overseeing the development of an eco-friendly retreat in Romania made from recycled shipping containers.

Having someone by your side who supports you even through the worst times makes all the difference in the world."

items.title: I libri scelti da Internazionale
items.summary: Da Il peggio arriva dopo di Mariana Enriquez a La pietra e la seta di Mikael Niemi. Le recensioni della stampa straniera Leggi
items.content:
Leggere Il peggio arriva dopo dell’argentina Mariana Enriquez è stato catartico. Sapevo di ritrovarmi tra quelle pagine, ma gli ultimi capitoli mi hanno colta alla sprovvista. Ho finito il libro un venerdì all’alba, dopo qualche bicchiere di birra, in una nuvola di fumo. Mi sono chiusa in bagno con il romanzo, in un gesto violento e disperato, tra le lacrime. È proprio come si dice: un romanzo di vampiri senza vampiri, che racconta la scena underground argentina degli anni novanta. I ribelli, i froci, gli strambi, i bellissimi, la bellezza luciferina e l’eterna adolescenza. L’innocenza manipolatrice di un enfant terrible come Rimbaud, come Facundo, e perturbazioni alla Lautréamont. È un romanzo adolescenziale, e non avrebbe potuto essere scritto altrimenti. Enriquez si abbandona al vagabondaggio giovanile, in un delirio di cocaina, marijuana e alcol, ma anche di amore, sesso e musica, che accompagna quelle notti buie e la repulsione per il sole e l’alba. A sconvolgermi sono state soprattutto le terribili allucinazioni di Narval, uno dei protagonisti, così profondamente legate alla sessualità. Narval mostra una certa sensibilità, Facundo, al contrario, un’indifferenza quasi assoluta. Eppure li unisce un amore goffo e traboccante, insieme a incubi che li trasformano in vampiri e li costringono a vivere di notte. È un libro che interroga i limiti dell’esistenza umana, un viaggio verso la dipendenza, l’amore e la morte. Enriquez non fugge dagli orrori: li evoca e li esorcizza. Beatriz A. Menelik, Alcantarilla

Quando il fratello maggiore eredita la fattoria di famiglia, Eino Vanhakoski rimane senza nulla ed è costretto a vivere di stenti nel nord svedese, al confine con la Finlandia. Privo di terra e impossibilitato a coltivarla, è alla mercé dei potenti della zona. Un affare che avrebbe dovuto arricchirlo, legato alla vendita di barili di catrame, finisce per gettare la sua giovane famiglia nella miseria. Il ricco proprietario terriero responsabile del disastro, invece, non subisce conseguenze. Il romanzo impiega un po’ a ingranare, ma diventa davvero interessante quando Eino, ormai sommerso dai debiti, è costretto a partecipare a una gara al ribasso per costruire una strada nella foresta. Sono gli anni in cui le idee socialiste e comuniste cominciano a radicarsi tra i lavoratori e l’arrivo di un sindacalista cambierà la vita dei Vanhakoski per generazioni. Chi non conosce la storia dei paesi nordici potrebbe pensare che siano sempre stati società egualitarie e prospere. Ma quell’immagine nasconde un passato di miseria e privazioni. Il romanzo racconta una Svezia lontanissima da quella che conosciamo oggi. In La pietra e la seta c’è anche una parte di trama ambientata nel 2017: un cadavere viene ritrovato in una palude e Siw, discendente dei Vanhakoski, ha delle visioni che la riportano ai segreti della famiglia. Questa parte distrae dalla storia principale e gli elementi soprannaturali sembrano poco sviluppati. Ma nel complesso è un romanzo avvincente, che aiuta a capire come sia nata la Svezia moderna. Michael O. Jones, Swedish Book Review

Si annuncia una serata memorabile al Zia Orsa, l’unico ristorante di alta cucina di una cittadina universitaria del midwest. Tra le prenotazioni c’è anche quella per una cena in onore di uno scrittore di enorme successo, John Grisham. Ma poche ore prima dell’apertura arriva una brutta sorpresa: ventidue bistecche sono scomparse dalla cella frigorifera. E il furto è chiaramente opera di qualcuno del personale. La prenotazione , il sesto romanzo di Rebecca Kauffman, è costruito come una serie di storie che s’intrecciano. Tutto si svolge nell’arco di un giorno e una notte, e ogni capitolo si concentra su uno dei dipendenti del ristorante, dal lavapiatti allo chef. Alcuni sembrano racconti autonomi, come quello di Edgar, che vive in macchina e fa due lavori per mandare soldi alla famiglia in Guatemala. Man mano che i legami tra i personaggi si complicano, tra gelosie professionali, rancori e storie d’amore, il ritmo accelera. Il romanzo alterna momenti di comicità quasi farsesca ad altri che sembrano piccole tragedie. Kauffman mostra quanto spesso i dipendenti del ristorante si giudichino a vicenda sulla base di pregiudizi che si rivelano infondati, invitandoci a riconsiderare le idee che abbiamo su chi lavora nei servizi. Norah Piehl, BookBrowse

“Solo il cuore sa che cos’è l’amore”, dice Ester Nilsson a un’amica in Uomini e donne , il romanzo dal titolo simbolico di Lena Andersson. “Se usi la ragione, non sei innamorato”. Nei romanzi precedenti della trilogia di Ester Nilsson, la protagonista cercava l’amore ed era pronta a sopportare quasi tutto, come in un melodramma scritto con il linguaggio di un verbale. Era questa contraddizione a dare forza alla scrittura. Ora i protagonisti sono persone mature, segnate dalla vita ma non disarmate. La ricerca dell’amore, e quanto ci sia concesso essere ciechi al primo sguardo e a tutti quelli successivi, è forse la favola più importante che raccontiamo a noi stessi. Questa volta la felicità arriva con il misterioso Paul Henning North, ed Ester la riconosce immediatamente. Crede che quasi tutto sia già dentro di noi, che non siamo noi a inventare il linguaggio e le norme. Il cuore sa, come ha scritto anche il romantico Karl Ove Knausgård. Anche lo stile un po’ fuori moda di Andersson seduce, spalancando le porte al novecento. Difetti? L’inserimento di alcune fastidiose mode linguistiche contemporanee e, a tratti, un tono da manuale di autoaiuto. Ulrika Milles, SVT Kultur

items.title: Setting Up SSH Keys on macOS with Touch ID
items.summary: Article URL: https://nmattia.com/posts/2026-10-19-setting-up-ssh-keys-touch-id/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50175882 Points: 26 # Comments: 18
items.content:
In the first part of this post I’ll show a simple, secure way to create an SSH key on Mac (it’s 3 commands, including support for GitHub). In the second part I’ll dig deeper and explain what’s actually happening for the curious reader.

Macs have a built-in so-called Secure Enclave , where we can create “identities” that simply cannot be stolen (unless maybe you’ve made enemies with a nation state). Those identities are protected with Touch ID and can be used for SSH authentication. There are some great benefits about using this over traditional SSH key files:

This extra security will be in effect whenever you use SSH, including git-over-ssh like GitHub. It’s great that advanced security tech is available by default on some of the most widely distributed computers in the world! A few years ago stuff like this could only be found at CERN and/or in Dan Brown novels. Let’s see how it can be set up on your consumer-grade Mac.

It is essential that the human interface be designed for ease of use, so that users routinely and automatically apply the protection mechanisms correctly.

We’ll create a secure identity on the Secure Enclave, then tell SSH how to use it for authentication, and finally add the key to GitHub.

You’ll be prompted to touch “Touch ID”. Your identity is now created and saved securely (parameters are explained in the deep dive below).

From here on, SSH will know to use the identity from the Secure Enclave when connecting via SSH; it does not have a good memory so you’ll need to remind it after a reboot.

If multiple identities are listed, use the line that starts with sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256... . It’s a shareable handle for the identity, and this is the SSH key that GitHub will ask about.

That’s all you need for a super secure setup! The new identity can now be used with SSH, and you’ll be prompted for Touch ID during authentication:

No one can steal your identity (well, you can’t even give it away willingly since it can’t be extracted from the Secure Enclave), but with great powers etc: if your Mac dies, so does the identity, and you’ll need to create a new one (and re-register it where necessary, like GitHub).

You’ll get a Touch ID prompt when git tries to authenticate with SSH

We’ll now try to understand what happens under the hood. We’ll start with the actual identity creation in the Secure Enclave, then look at how SSH is allowed to interface with the Secure Enclave with ssh-keychain.dylib , and then try to see what happens in a complete SSH sign-in flow.

This is the result of reading posts (like this great investigation by arianvp ), manual pages, and experimentation. A lot of this is undocumented, and this is the minimum information I needed to form a mental model of what’s happening and convince myself that it does, indeed, work.

Some of the command outputs below have been trimmed for legibility, I invite you to run them locally if you want the full experience!

Identities are managed with the sc_auth command (where sc_ stands for Smart Card). In Apple-speak, they are “CryptoTokenKit” identities, or CTK identities for short. Why not Smart Card Identities? What is a Smart Card? No idea! There’s a lot of weird Apple vocabulary, but in practice they’re just private keys stored on the Secure Enclave:

If you followed along in the Quick Setup , you should have exactly one identity here, that was created when you ran the sc_auth create-ctk-identity command. Let’s look at the create-ctk-identity command in more detail:

When using the p-256-ne key type, this command creates the identity on the Secure Enclave — I’m guessing by first gathering some entropy, then generating some private key material and allocating whatever it needs for bookkeeping and ensuring it can only be accessed with your fingerprint.

The label is freeform and just a note attached to the key. The key type is a cryptographic setting (the elliptic curve used). At the time of writing, the following values are accepted: p-256|p-384|p-521|p-256-ne|p-384-ne . The -ne suffix means “Non-Extractable”, meaning the key is generated by the enclave itself and cannot be extracted from the Secure Enclave. For SSH we only need signing , which is done by (and on ) the Secure Enclave itself, and at no point do we need (or want) to export the private key. The p-384 curve is not supported by (Open)SSH, so this narrows it down to p-256-ne .

Finally, protection can be either bio or none . When set to bio , using the key requires biometrics (like Touch ID). With none , the key still cannot be extracted (i.e. stolen) but programs would be able to silently use SSH; I recommend using bio , but YMMV; if you get annoyed by the Touch ID prompts whenever you git pull , you might want to use none here.

Now that we have some elusive identity on the Secure Enclave, let’s see how we can tell SSH to use it for authentication.

There’s a bit of impedance mismatch, and ssh doesn’t know how to use the identity by default:

The SSH agent cannot use the Secure Enclave identities as-is, but Apple has us covered with a small translation layer in the form of ssh-keychain.dylib , a dlopen -able library available natively on all recent macOS versions:

Here we’re relying on ssh-add ’s built-in support for FIDO-style authenticator via the -K parameter. This lets the SSH agent know that it shouldn’t read a standard private key (for instance ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ) but that it should expect the keys to be stored “externally” (for a lack of better words). With -K alone, ssh-add would look for public keys on USB devices (think YubiKey); though we can customize this behavior by registering a “security key provider” with -S . This provider should be a stateless dynamically-loadable library, which is exactly what /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib is. The interface is not documented (at least not in a way I was able to meaningfully process), but we can have a look at what ssh-keychain.dylib exposes:

Most likely, _sk_load_resident_keys is meant to return a list of (public keys of) identities, and _sk_sign will sign a payload using a specified identity (here, resident means “residing on e.g. the Secure Enclave”).

We’ve seen how the identities can be created on the Secure Enclave, and how they can, in theory, be used by the SSH agent. Let’s put this to the test and see what happens when an SSH connection is created.

Let’s see what we need for authenticating to a remote SSH server. At all times, the SSH agent needs (1) a list of (public) keys that can be used to authenticate, and (2) a way to prove to a server that it has the corresponding private key for any of those keys.

When ssh-add is first called with -S , the _sk_load_resident_keys routine is called, which returns the public keys of all resident keys on the FIDO-style authenticator. Those are stored in the SSH agent (alongside their corresponding provider, namely ssh-keychain.dylib ) and will later be offered as candidates to any remote SSH server we try connecting to. (Also now that the SSH agent knows about the Secure Enclave identity we created earlier, we can view its SSH-style public key with ssh-add -L .)

Let’s say an SSH connection is initiated: the remote accepts one of those public keys offered by the agent and “challenges” the client to prove its identity. The agent calls _sk_sign to create a signature with the private key (matching the accepted public key) and the challenge (roughly speaking). This will be forwarded to the Secure Enclave, prompt Touch ID, and if approved, will return a signature for the challenge. The signature is forwarded back to the server, which can confirm we — the client — have the corresponding private key.

The ssh debug logs show that one key is offered by the agent, accepted, and then used to create a signature. After the server has verified the signature, authentication is granted (although GitHub does not provide shell access ).

One note: whenever we register the identity with the SSH agent, ssh-add prompts us for a PIN. What gives? Why does entering an empty PIN work, isn’t this mighty unsafe‽

Well, no, it’s not unsafe! When we tell ssh-add to use a FIDO-style authenticator, I suspect its default behavior is to ask for a PIN as it assumes we’ll be using a USB, YubiKey-style authenticator; only we shortcut the whole thing with ssh-keychain.dylib (and the security comes not from a PIN, but from the soft skin under your fingertips; much cooler). Not great in terms of usability, but I guess it makes sense. (I have no idea what would happen if you have more than one FIDO authenticator; go support me on GitHub and I’ll buy a collection of YubiKeys to experiment).

Let’s recap: we can use a somewhat cryptic, poorly documented “Smart Card” tool to create a “CryptoTokenKit” identity on the “Secure Enclave”. Then, by using the poorly documented ssh-keychain.dylib , we can use said identity to generate signatures that Apple’s ssh can use. There’s no guarantee that all this missing documentation wouldn’t say “Do not use this; terribly unsafe in practice”, but hey: all this security talk by Apple, they wouldn’t lie to us, right? *spooky*

items.title: 'Trash Island' or DC landmark? How a golf course got Trump in a messy legal dispute
items.summary: Trump said he has plans to turn a 106-year-old public golf course in Washington DC into a tournament-capable golf course for pros, but local golfers are not happy.
items.content:
For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.

"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.

But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.

Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".

The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.

Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space.

Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".

But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans.

The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation.

"Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media.

The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice.

A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday.

While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement".

Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access.

The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms.

Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city.

"You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said.

As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac.

"There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said.

Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out.

"Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.

items.title: I data center e i bot russi
items.summary: Le infrastrutture su cui si reggono non solo le intelligenze artificiali ma anche tutto l’ecosistema digitale sono ormai obiettivi strategici e militari Leggi
items.content:
L’8 ottobre 2026 alcuni droni ucraini hanno colpito un data center della Yandex, l’azienda che gestisce il principale motore di ricerca russo. L’attacco è avvenuto a Sasovo, nella regione di Rjazan, circa trecento chilometri a sudest di Mosca. Il giorno dopo è toccato a un impianto a Kaluga, a sudovest della capitale. L’11 ottobre, infine, la Yandex ha comunicato di aver chiuso anche il suo data center nella regione di Vladimir dopo un altro attacco. Secondo Cybernews , gli impianti di Sasovo e di Vladimir sono ancora fermi e a Kaluga una parte delle macchine è inutilizzabile.

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelenskyj ha detto che questi attacchi sono una reazione ad altri bombardamenti fatti dai russi sui data center ucraini.

Le infrastrutture su cui si reggono non solo le intelligenze artificiali ma anche tutto l’ecosistema digitale sono ormai obiettivi strategici e militari. È una questione di cui bisognerebbe tenere conto quando si decide dove costruirle e come farle.

Questa notizia, però, oltre a ricordarci le strutture materiali che permettono ai servizi digitali di esistere e funzionare, ha preso anche un’altra piega inaspettata. Su X e su Bluesky ha cominciato a circolare un grafico di Cloudflare Radar , il servizio con cui la Cloudflare osserva il traffico di internet. Il grafico mostra il crollo delle richieste automatiche partite dalla rete della Yandex, scese allo 0,4 per cento del picco delle due settimane precedenti.

Da questo dato si è arrivati a un salto logico: è bastato bombardare tre data center per fermare la propaganda dell’internazionale nera, che evidentemente viene dalla Russia.

Secondo lo storico statunitense Timothy Snyder , a giudicare dai dati di quel giorno, gran parte dei bot che pubblicano contenuti a favore di Donald Trump negli Stati Uniti e di Alternative für Deutschland (Afd) sembrava dipendere direttamente dai data center russi. Il deputato europeo ceco Tomáš Zdechovský ha condiviso un’immagine che mostrava il crollo dell’attività online intorno all’Afd. Molte persone hanno cominciato a dire che effettivamente sembrava che ci fosse meno disinformazione russa, a giudicare da quel che vedevano dai loro account.

Il 12 ottobre lo stesso Zelenskyj ha cavalcato questa lettura sostenendo che quando i droni hanno raggiunto i data center della Yandex, usare i social media è diventato all’improvviso più facile, perché i bot erano diminuiti. Secondo lui, a quel punto era abbastanza chiaro da dove arrivassero.

Ma è proprio così? Prima di tutto, si è scoperto che l’immagine condivisa dal deputato non era vera . Lo ha spiegato, fra gli altri, antibot4navalny , un account che da anni segue le campagne coordinate della propaganda di stato russa. Funziona così: Cloudflare Radar registra le richieste che arrivano ai siti protetti dalla Cloudflare e assegna a ciascuna un punteggio, che stima la probabilità che a generarla sia stato un programma automatico.

Tuttavia, nel caso della Yandex quei programmi sono soprattutto crawler , cioè software che visitano le pagine per indicizzarle e raccogliere dati, anche per le intelligenze artificiali. È il modo in cui funziona normalmente un motore di ricerca.

Il grafico racconta quindi che per qualche giorno il motore di ricerca russo ha visitato molto meno i siti occidentali. Ma non ci dà alcuna informazione su chi paga gli account falsi, chi diffonde propaganda, né su cosa succede su X o su Facebook.

Fra l’altro, nella settimana degli attacchi il traffico automatico complessivo dalla Russia misurato dalla Cloudflare è rimasto simile a quello delle settimane precedenti e il traffico della Yandex ha ripreso a salire lentamente già domenica 11 ottobre. Non solo: è dal 2022 che piattaforme come Reddit e Facebook bloccano le connessioni che arrivano direttamente dai data center delle aziende russe. Per questo le operazioni di propaganda passano da reti di proxy residenziali, dispositivi violati, vpn commerciali e servizi cloud occidentali, che nascondono la vera origine del traffico. Hadi Ghanbari, esperto di guerra cibernetica, ha detto a Newsweek che è difficile stabilire se le campagne condotte con account falsi abbiano subìto qualche danno.

E così sono arrivate le prime retromarce: l’eurodeputato ceco Zdechovský ha ammesso di non avere prove che gli attacchi fossero collegati a un calo dell’attività delle reti di disinformazione russe. Alla Bbc, un portavoce di Zelenskyj ha detto che il presidente ucraino si riferiva genericamente “all’atmosfera sui social media”.

Le affermazioni sullo spegnimento dei bot russi, insomma, sono nella migliore delle ipotesi esagerate. Nella peggiore sono false. Caroline Orr Bueno, scienziata comportamentale che studia la disinformazione, ha scritto che chi vuole difendere la democrazia deve rifiutare la disinformazione anche quando racconta la storia che vorrebbe sentirsi raccontare. Un progetto online sta sottoponendo a verifica sistematica tutto quello che è stato detto in merito.

Questa storia ci insegna che, purtroppo, la propaganda funziona quando conferma quello che crediamo già. Vale per chi sta con Mosca e vale per chi sta con Kiev. E la scorciatoia è sempre a portata di mano, per esempio chiamare “bot di disinformazione russa” tutto quello che ci dà fastidio online, mettendo nello stesso calderone i programmi che indicizzano il web e gli account coordinati che manipolano le conversazioni.

Chi potrebbe chiudere la questione? Gli unici in grado di dire se l’attività degli account di disinformazione è calata davvero sono le piattaforme. Però la X di Elon Musk nel 2023 ha chiuso l’accesso gratuito ai suoi dati, usato da molti ricercatori. E la Meta nel 2024 ha spento CrowdTangle, lo strumento con cui giornalisti e studiosi seguivano la circolazione dei contenuti su Facebook. Il Digital services act europeo prevede che le grandi piattaforme aprano i dati ai ricercatori accreditati, ma la strada per arrivarci è lenta.

Se davvero vogliamo capire cosa succede nella guerra dell’informazione, servono dati pubblici e verificabili e una ricerca indipendente in grado di usarli. Fra l’altro, con le intelligenze artificiali che abbiamo a disposizione l’analisi di questi dati sarebbe particolarmente semplice da fare e anche molto efficace. Solo che oggi a decidere cosa possiamo sapere sono sempre le solite poche aziende private (spesso le stesse che producono ia) e hanno deciso che questi dati non li dobbiamo avere. Così, quel vuoto informativo viene riempito dal primo grafico condiviso, purché racconti la storia nel modo in cui piace a noi.

items.title: Le donne palestinesi sono sole di fronte alle violenze
items.summary: Il rapporto di un’agenzia delle Nazioni Unite ha documentato un aumento di abusi fisici ed emotivi, sfruttamento sessuale e matrimoni precoci ai danni delle donne sfollate a Gaza Leggi
items.content:
L’agenzia delle Nazioni Unite per la salute sessuale e riproduttiva (Unfpa) ha pubblicato un rapporto basato sulle conversazioni avute con 230 donne palestinesi sfollate a Gaza, facendo luce sul fenomeno in gran parte trascurato della violenza sessuale e dell’oppressione di genere nei luoghi in cui vivono le persone che hanno perso la casa.

Quello della violenza domestica è stato un tema ricorrente nelle discussioni di gruppo. Le donne hanno descritto abusi fisici ed emotivi da parte di mariti, figli, fratelli e suoceri. Hanno anche raccontato casi di sfruttamento sessuale, stupro da parte del coniuge, matrimoni precoci o forzati, abusi, limitazioni alla libertà di movimento, furto dei pacchi di aiuti e minacce di vedersi portare via i figli rimasti orfani del padre. Tutto questo avviene in luoghi sovraffollati dove non esiste praticamente alcuna forma di privacy.

Il rapporto, scritto e pubblicato a settembre dall’Unfpa, non quantifica l’incidenza degli abusi nei campi per sfollati né fa una stima del numero di vittime. Si concentra piuttosto sul fenomeno, dando voce alle 230 donne che hanno partecipato. Non è basato su un campione rappresentativo e le minorenni non hanno partecipato; le donne coinvolte avevano tra i diciotto e i 63 anni.

Secondo il rapporto, le donne sono particolarmente vulnerabili alle aggressioni di estranei nelle lunghe code per l’acqua, nei punti di distribuzione del cibo e degli aiuti e nei servizi igienici. Secondo le testimonianze, alcuni uomini approfittano delle file per strusciarsi contro le donne. Bagni e docce sono spesso condivisi tra famiglie non imparentate tra loro e lì sono stati documentati casi di molestie sessuali e perfino stupri.

La ricerca sul campo e le interviste, realizzate tra dicembre 2025 e gennaio 2026 nell’ambito di sedici focus group, sono state condotte dal Women’s affairs center, un’organizzazione femminista indipendente fondata nel 1991 per supportare le donne e consolidare la loro condizione individuale e collettiva nella società palestinese. Le testimonianze e le riflessioni raccolte durante le conversazioni sono state analizzate dall’Acaps Middle East analysis hub, un’organizzazione specializzata nell’analisi di dati in situazioni di crisi umanitaria, con sede ad Amman.

Alle donne coinvolte non è stato chiesto di rivelare esperienze personali e a volte hanno usato un linguaggio indiretto o mitigato per descrivere le violenze. In cinque focus group le partecipanti hanno raccontato di essere venute a conoscenza di casi in cui i soldati israeliani hanno aggredito sessualmente le donne che attraversavano i checkpoint militari mentre fuggivano dai bombardamenti verso le aree designate come umanitarie.

Gli autori del rapporto ipotizzano che le donne abbiano evitato di parlare delle violenze commessse dai combattenti palestinesi, sia esponenti di Hamas sia delle milizie appoggiate da Israele nella Striscia di Gaza, per timore di ritorsioni o di stigmatizzazione sociale. “I risultati non consentono dunque di trarre conclusioni sull’incidenza, o l’assenza, di violenze di genere compiute da soggetti armati palestinesi”, afferma il rapporto.

Le facilitatrici dei focus group, le partecipanti e gli autori del rapporto sono consapevoli che la violenza contro le donne non è un fenomeno nuovo. Ma dalle conversazioni emerge chiaramente un significativo aumento nella diffusione e nelle forme di violenza e oppressione da quando è iniziata la guerra. In tutti i gruppi le donne hanno raccontato di partner che non erano mai stati violenti e hanno cominciato a maltrattarle a causa dello stress provocato dalle perdite, dalla povertà e dallo sfollamento. In una discussione una donna dell’area di Gaza ha detto: “Mio marito non aveva mai alzato la voce contro di me prima della guerra. Ma da quando la nostra casa è stata bombardata e abbiamo perso tutto quello che avevamo è diventato irritabile e ora se la prende con me e con i bambini”.

Allo stesso tempo, osserva il rapporto, le donne non hanno alcun posto dove rifugiarsi e nessuno a cui chiedere aiuto. Lo sfollamento forzato ha scardinato le strutture di sostegno familiari e di comunità. Le istituzioni ufficiali che dovrebbero garantire protezione, come la polizia, i tribunali e gli uffici dei servizi sociali, non funzionano più: sono state bombardate, si trovano in aree sotto il controllo militare israeliano o sono difficili e costose da raggiungere a causa delle strade distrutte.

Anche i meccanismi comunitari di soluzione delle controversie hanno perso la loro influenza. Secondo le testimonianze, oggi questi meccanismi tendono a salvaguardare la “pace familiare” piuttosto che mettere fine alla violenza. Inoltre, in questi anni Israele ha impedito di operare nella Striscia alle organizzazioni umanitarie internazionali con una consolidata esperienza di supporto psicologico alle donne.

Tutte le partecipanti hanno raccontato di essere state sfollate tra le due e le dieci volte, con una media di sette. Le discussioni si sono svolte nelle città di Gaza e Khan Yunis. Circa 1,1 milioni di persone sfollate, di cui 480mila donne e ragazze, vivono in queste due aree, in centinaia di insediamenti, nelle tendopoli o in edifici scolastici. Ci sono 428 insediamenti di questo tipo nella città di Gaza e 516 a Khan Yunis, che ospitano in totale più di 840mila sfollati. In circa il 40 per cento dei campi e degli insediamenti manca un organismo ufficiale responsabile dell’illuminazione, della manutenzione dei bagni e delle docce comuni e della sicurezza, a cui rivolgersi per lamentele o denunce. Nelle discussioni l’assenza di un organismo simile è stato associato a un forte senso di insicurezza.

Le donne hanno spiegato che il matrimonio a Gaza può essere una possibilità di sopravvivenza, ma anche un mezzo di sfruttamento. Dai racconti emergono varie forme di matrimonio forzato: accordi tra famiglie senza il consenso della donna, vedove costrette a sposare il cognato e unioni tra una vittima di violenza sessuale e il suo stupratore, o un altro uomo. “Quando si scoprono casi di stupro in una scuola” usata come rifugio, “il giorno dopo in quella struttura si vedono matrimoni e festeggiamenti”, ha raccontato una donna che vive a Khan Yunis.

I matrimoni precoci e forzati non sono un fenomeno nuovo a Gaza. Nel 2019-2020 circa un quarto delle donne sposate di età compresa tra i 20 e i 49 anni si era sposata prima di compiere diciotto anni. Tuttavia, il rapporto sottolinea che la diffusione dei matrimoni precoci era in calo. Dall’inizio della guerra, invece, sono aumentati i matrimoni di minorenni e le gravidanze tra le adolescenti.

Le partecipanti hanno spiegato che il matrimonio precoce può essere incentivato dall’offerta di sacchi di farina o di una tenda in cambio di una sposa bambina. Hanno anche legato i matrimoni precoci alla distruzione delle scuole e al collasso del sistema educativo, nonostante i tentativi di garantire un’istruzione negli insediamenti per sfollati. Accade anche, al contrario, che i familiari si oppongano al matrimonio di una donna nubile che lavora per poter continuare a contare sul suo reddito.

Le più vulnerabili allo sfruttamento economico o sessuale, alla limitazione dell’autonomia e ai maltrattamenti sono vedove, divorziate e separate, donne con disabilità e anziane. Secondo il rapporto, vedove e divorziate sono particolarmente esposte a forme di ricatto sessuale degli uomini che controllano l’accesso alle risorse essenziali, come acqua, assistenza sanitaria, farmaci e viveri.

Denunce di molestie sessuali nei centri per sfollati erano emerse anche durante le precedenti guerre di Israele a Gaza. Da quando nel 2023 è cominciato l’attuale conflitto, le ulteriori difficoltà che le donne sono costrette ad affrontare rispetto agli uomini sono state ampiamente documentate. Tra queste ci sono la necessità di restare coperte anche in situazioni di caldo estremo a causa della mancanza di spazi privati, di fare meno docce per timore di molestie, di evitare i servizi igienici di notte e di non trovare assorbenti.

Anche nelle prime fasi della guerra si era parlato dell’aumento di matrimoni precoci e di gravidanze tra adolescenti a causa degli stupri o delle scarse conoscenze in materia di salute sessuale. Eppure si è registrata una tendenza, o un’aspettativa, a non discutere questi fenomeni in modo approfondito né in pubblico né sui mezzi d’informazione. I promotori e le partecipanti alla ricerca sperano che questa situazione possa cambiare. ◆

items.title: Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/attack-surface-reduction Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50175779 Points: 16 # Comments: 4
items.content:
Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability.

Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. With these results in mind, we discuss how developers can apply similar techniques to their own code.

Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another. This can often cause it to function very differently to how its original developers intended. And it is a big part of why attackers are often so successful: they study exactly how a piece of code behaves in practice, rather than how its developers intended or designed it to work.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction techniques aim to discover unnecessary attack surfaces, then move that code behind an appropriate gate. This might involve moving code from pre-authentication to post-authentication, from 0-click to 1-click, from on-by-default to explicit opt-in, or from the first message of a protocol to deeper in the session state machine. Some code is meant to be reachable before these stages, but a lot it is not, and, given the complexity that comes with code churn across thousands or millions of lines of code, unnecessary exposure of features often goes unnoticed.

There are numerous ways to reduce the attack surface of code. In our own research efforts, we focused on three methods in particular:

We wanted to understand how well Claude could take these three descriptions of attack surface and discover real issues in large and complex codebases. We analyzed 25 open source projects (representing over five million lines of code), written in languages including C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python. Claude created an inventory of over 17,000 configuration options across these projects. Of those, 3,842 related to the configuration of a control or feature that was security relevant.

For the purposes of our research, we broke down these open source projects into three broad categories:

These categories help to contextualize our results. For example, we’d expect a significant percentage of a Public codebase to be reachable in the default configuration (since it’s designed to serve any user), but the opposite to be true for projects in the Gated category.

Claude found 493 issues using the three methods described above. Several themes stuck out to us from its results.

First, Claude found that all eleven gated projects had code that was unintentionally reachable (although this code wasn’t a significant percentage of the total lines of code for any of those projects). Specifically, Claude discovered 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces in the default configuration of the gated cohort, 37 locations where code executed, or state was recorded, before authentication, and 61 configuration combinations that silently weakened a pre-authentication control configured by the administrator. None of these issues would have been immediately exploitable on their own, but they create a much larger attack surface than is necessary.

Second, Claude’s work mitigating configuration interaction issues produced some of the most interesting and impactful findings (across all project types). Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction. In 94 of those cases, the combination silently turned off a security control. The other 68 cases were inconsistencies in the same security mechanisms (e.g. a listener or login path would remain reachable even though the configuration would say it was disabled; two settings would conflict, and the one that would take precedence would depend on their order in the configuration file, or a protection configured by the administrator would do nothing while its code remained reachable). While some of these configuration combinations might be non-standard or infrequently used, there would be nothing preventing an administrator of these projects from configuring and deploying the code in this way.

Claude also found one specific pattern that turned up independently in four unrelated projects. This would work as follows. An administrator would write an access rule for remote clients using a hostname or a wildcard pattern, instead of an IP address. When a client connects, the server would compare that rule against the client’s hostname. Whether the server ever learned that hostname would depend on a separate option that controlled reverse DNS lookups (which most projects had configured off). With lookups off, the server would only have the client’s IP address. The server would compare the rule against that address as plain text. But a hostname pattern can never match an IP address. This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open. Some of the affected projects mention in their documentation that hostname rules depend on DNS lookups being enabled, but none state that a deny list written this way would have fail open behavior.

Third, Claude often discovered that two configuration options would conflict in a way that silently dropped a security check. In one case, an administrator could require every connecting client to prove its identity with a certificate. In another, the code was only intended to delay that check until it was required, but in fact disabled the check entirely. A server that was configured to accept only trusted clients would therefore accept a connection from anyone. This exposed a large body of request handling code (which was supposed to be behind the certificate check) to unauthenticated clients. The software accepted both configuration options together with no warning under default settings; the documentation never mentioned that the certificate requirement had been dropped. This conflicting set of configuration options had been present in the software for 21 years.

Finally, Claude discovered an issue in a project that left authentication off by default (and expected the administrator to turn it on). The option that required TLS client certificates was honored on most of the project’s network endpoints, but silently ignored on a few others (ones which loaded their TLS settings through a path with a different namespace). This meant that a client with no certificate could complete the TLS handshake and open a session on an affected endpoint. Nothing would be logged about the ignored setting. Whether the option takes effect would depend on the namespace used by the administrator in the configuration. One form of the setting name works on every endpoint, but the shorter form—which most examples use—is dropped on the affected ones.

Surprisingly, when measured as a percentage of the total lines of code, the project for which Claude achieved the largest reduction in attack surface was OpenSSH. OpenSSH is a high quality C codebase that provides secure remote access. Claude traced the input paths of the SSH daemon in the 10.4 release and found roughly 4,500 lines of new and experimental code for ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum signature algorithm, that an unauthenticated client could reach in the default configuration. ML-DSA is not enabled by default, but the code was reachable regardless, even when an administrator explicitly excluded the algorithm. The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed. There is no good reason for this complex, memory unsafe code to be reachable when it hasn’t been enabled by the configuration. Those 4,500 lines of code in ML-DSA-44 are about 16% of OpenSSH’s own pre-authentication code in a default sshd. We reported this to the OpenSSH developers along with patches. The 10.5 release moved the check before parsing.
